In the Supreme Court of the United States

(1)
In the Supreme Court of the United States
───────────
No. 26A560
MARKWAYNE MULLIN, SECRETARY OF HOMELAND SECURITY, ET AL., APPLICANTS
v.
FRIENDS OF THE RUIDOSA CHURCH, ET AL.
───────────
REPLY IN SUPPORT OF APPLICATION FOR A STAY OF THE
INJUNCTION ISSUED BY THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE WESTERN DISTRICT OF TEXAS
───────────
A stay is plainly warranted of this unprecedented injunction enjoining the Sec-
retary’s waivers and indefinitely barring border-wall construction across at least a
quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border.  To begin, the government is exceedingly likely to
succeed on the merits.  Congress stripped district courts of jurisdiction to entertain
non-constitutional challenges to the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decisions to
waive legal requirements when necessary to facilitate border-wall construction.  Yet
the district court enjoined the Secretary’s waivers by invoking the major-questions
doctrine in service of a claim that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority un-
der IIRIRA.  See Appl. App. 214a.  Respondents’ rejoinder—that the major-questions
doctrine has “constitutional underpinnings,” Opp. 15—does not transform the doc-
trine into a constitutional challenge.
Not only are respondents trying to turn a major-questions claim into a consti-
tutional challenge, but their major-questions claim is really a disguised, run-of-the-
mill dispute over the meaning of express statutory terms, and a flawed one to boot.
Congress undisputedly and expressly did confer on the Secretary the power to “waive

2
all legal requirements” in order to facilitate border-barrier construction as he deems
necessary “to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry,” IIRIRA § 102(a),
110 Stat. 3009-554; IIRIRA § 102(c)(1), as amended, 119 Stat. 306, and Secretaries
have long issued such waivers.  Unlike ordinary major-questions cases, respondents
and the district court dispute the scope of that authority, not its existence, contending
that the Big Bend sector does not qualify as an area of “high illegal entry” because
other sectors have higher apprehension rates.  That argument misconstrues the text,
which does not compel a comparative analysis, and only underscores the extent to
which respondents are trying to parlay a garden-variety statutory argument into a
constitutional challenge.
The equities also strongly favor the government.  Though respondents assert
that the government will not be irreparably harmed absent a stay, Opp. 23-31, even
the district court found that the government “will experience at least some degree of
irreparable harm.”  Appl. App. 236a.  The district court simply understated the
harms.  Not only will the government be irreparably harmed from being unable to
implement the border-wall waivers that Congress prescribed, to advance critical sov-
ereign interests of controlling the border, but the record also includes specific, sub-
stantial evidence showing public-safety and operational harms from this injunction.
See id. at 218a-232a.  Respondents quibble with the pace and extent of border-wall
construction, deeming existing border infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector adequate
to protect public safety and secure the border.  See Opp. 25-29.  But those policy de-
terminations belong to the Secretary, not to respondents or the courts.
Against the government’s serious injuries, respondents assert aesthetic, envi-
ronmental, and spiritual interests in preserving the Big Bend region.  Opp. 31-37.
The government has already explained that its construction in public recreational

3
areas will be limited.  See Appl. 33.  In all events, Congress has already determined
that such interests are outweighed by the government’s interests in constructing bor-
der infrastructure.  That is why it authorized the Secretary to waive environmental
and preservation laws as needed to build border barriers and roads.  A stay is over-
whelmingly warranted.  And the district court’s errors in this case are so clear, and
the consequences of its injunction so grave, that this Court should construe the ap-
plication as a petition for a writ of certiorari, grant the petition, and summarily re-
verse to avoid unnecessarily prolonging proceedings.
A.
The Government Is Highly Likely To Succeed On The Merits
The injunction is fatally flawed on the merits for multiple independent reasons.
See Appl. 15-24.  Respondents’ rejoinders are unpersuasive and only underscore why
summary disposition of this straightforward claim is warranted here.
1.
The district court exceeded its jurisdiction
a.
All agree that federal jurisdiction over IIRIRA waiver decisions is lim-
ited to claims “alleging a violation of the Constitution.”  IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(A).  But
as respondents acknowledge, the major-questions doctrine “operates to interpret a
statutory grant of authority.”  Opp. 15 (emphasis added).  And executive assertions of
authority that fail the major-questions doctrine exceed statutory authority.  That
alone shows that the jurisdictional bar plainly applies.
Respondents contend that because the major-questions doctrine has “constitu-
tional underpinnings,” Opp. 15, they have alleged a constitutional violation.  But they
ignore the flaws in that logic.  See Appl. 18.  Many canons for interpreting statutes
have constitutional underpinnings, from the federalism canon to the clear-statement
rule for abrogating sovereign immunity.  Just because a court relies on a canon with
constitutional overtones does not mean that it has adjudicated an alleged constitu-

4
tional violation.  The canon of constitutional avoidance is a prime example:  It has
constitutional underpinnings but exists “to avoid the decision of constitutional ques-
tions.”  Clark v. Martinez, 543 U.S. 371, 381-382 (2005).  A litigant who relies on
constitutional avoidance is seeking “to vindicate his own statutory rights”—hence,
invoking constitutional avoidance is “not a method of adjudicating constitutional
questions by other means.”  Id. at 381.  Respondents offer no response, let alone any
explanation for why the major-questions doctrine alone should be viewed differently.
This Court’s decision in Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462 (1994), further refutes
respondents’ argument.  Dalton explained that “claims simply alleging that the Pres-
ident has exceeded his statutory authority are not ‘constitutional’ claims.”  Id. at 473.
But that is what respondents allege here.  See, e.g., Opp. 19 (arguing that “the Big
Bend Waivers amount to an unprecedented interpretation of IIRIRA”); Opp. 20 (con-
tending that “the statute [i.e. IIRIRA] grants no such authority” for the Big Bend
waivers).  Were there a major-questions exception to Dalton, as respondents appar-
ently envision (Opp. 16), plaintiffs could label any garden-variety statutory claims as
major-questions claims and “broaden[ ] beyond recognition” the limits Congress care-
fully drew on jurisdiction over challenges to IIRIRA waivers, Dalton, 511 U.S. at
474—as respondents do here, see pp. 6-9, infra.
b.
Respondents try to give their claim a constitutional gloss by analogizing
the major-questions doctrine to the nondelegation doctrine.  Opp. 15-16.  They con-
tend that the major-questions and nondelegation doctrines are “two sides of the same
coin” because both guard “against overexpansive delegations of Congress’s legislative
power.”  Ibid.  Respondents’ focus on the doctrines’ overlapping purposes ignores the
critical differences in how the doctrines operate.  A nondelegation claim actually al-
leges that Congress has violated the Constitution by delegating Article I powers else-

5
where.  See Whitman v. American Trucking Ass’ns, 531 U.S. 457, 472 (2001).  A major-
questions claim, by contrast, avoids the need to determine whether Congress has vi-
olated Article I by alleging that Congress did not actually grant the power that the
Executive has asserted.  The major-questions doctrine is thus used to determine
whether a statute has been violated, not whether there has been a constitutional vi-
olation.  See Appl. 16 (collecting examples).
Respondents further argue that the major-questions and nondelegation doc-
trines both “operate[ ] through statutory interpretation.”  Opp. 15.  They cite the plu-
rality’s observation in Gundy v. United States, 588 U.S. 128, 135 (2019), that “a non-
delegation inquiry always begins (and often almost ends) with statutory interpreta-
tion.”  But in a nondelegation challenge, that is because the statutory-interpretation
inquiry as to whether Congress provided an intelligible principle to constrain execu-
tive implementation is dispositive of whether Congress violated Article I.  See id. at
136 (“Only after a court has determined a challenged statute’s meaning can it decide
whether the law sufficiently guides executive discretion to accord with Article I.”).  In
a major-questions case, by contrast, the “central” and ultimate inquiry is whether the
Executive Branch’s claimed power is “supported by clear statutory authority.”  Learn-
ing Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229, 283 (2026) (Gorsuch, J., concurring).
Respondents ultimately give away the game by asking this Court in a footnote
to resolve this case on nondelegation, not major-question, grounds—an implicit
acknowledgement that the doctrines are distinct.  Opp. 16 n.8.  Underscoring that
point, respondents pleaded major-questions violations and nondelegation violations
as separate counts.  See D. Ct. Doc. 26, at 39 (Aug. 11, 2026) (alleging nondelegation-
doctrine violation “in the alternative” to major-questions-doctrine violation) (capital-
ization omitted).  Regardless, it is too late for respondents to switch horses; the major-

6
questions claim is the sole basis for the injunction.  See Appl. App. 214a.  The district
court did not decide whether respondents were likely to succeed on their separate
nondelegation claim, id. at 215a n.4—a claim that other courts have uniformly re-
jected.  See, e.g., Center for Biological Diversity v. McAleenan, 404 F. Supp. 3d 218,
249 (D.D.C. 2019) (K.B. Jackson, J.), cert. denied, 591 U.S. 1015 (2020).
2.
The major-questions doctrine does not foreclose the Big Bend
waivers
Even if the district court had jurisdiction over respondents’ major-questions
claim, it is meritless.  Appl. 19-24.
a.
This is not a major-questions case.  The major-questions doctrine pro-
vides that when the government seeks to decide a question of “vast economic and
political significance” or to assert “extravagant statutory power over the national
economy,” courts must look for a “clear” indication that Congress actually intended
to delegate the asserted authority.  West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 716, 723-724
(2022) (citations omitted).  Here, Congress unambiguously delegated to the Secretary
the power to “waive all legal requirements” that he “determines necessary to ensure
expeditious construction” of border barriers and roads under IIRIRA Section 102.
IIRIRA § 102(c)(1); see Appl. 20.  That authority is perfectly clear.
  Respondents nevertheless contend that the Big Bend waivers trigger the ma-
jor-questions doctrine because the construction facilitated by those waivers will be
costly.  See Opp. 17.  But the major-questions doctrine does not reflexively apply an-
ytime the government engages in an expensive construction project.  The doctrine
applies only in “extraordinary cases” “representing a ‘transformative expansion’ ” in
the government’s “ ‘regulatory authority.’ ”  West Virginia, 597 U.S. at 724 (citation
omitted).  There is nothing “extraordinary” or “transformative” about the Secretary’s

7
use of his clear Section 102(c) waiver authority.  On the contrary, CBP counts over 60
IIRIRA waiver decisions to facilitate border-wall construction since Congress gave
DHS that power in 2005.  See Appl. 9.  The Big Bend waivers are merely a recent
example of the Secretary using a well-worn tool in his border-security toolkit.
Respondents try to differentiate the Big Bend waivers as “unprecedented” in
their “scale, size, and purpose.”  Opp. 18.  That, too, is wrong.  In 2008, the Secretary
issued a waiver decision “to facilitate construction of barriers and roads along 470
miles of the United States-Mexico border in Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and Cali-
fornia.”  County of El Paso v. Chertoff, No. 08-CA-196, 2008 WL 4372693 (W.D. Tex.
Aug. 29, 2008) (discussing 73 Fed. Reg. 19,078 (Apr. 8, 2008)).  That single waiver
decision encompassed project areas spanning more miles of the border than any of
the three Big Bend waivers, and in fact covered an area equivalent to about 75% of
the number of border miles covered by all three Big Bend waivers combined.  Other
waiver decisions have likewise covered significant swaths of the border.  See, e.g., 90
Fed. Reg. 57,088 (Dec. 9, 2025) (waiver for project areas in the Rio Grande Valley
spanning about 277 miles).  The Big Bend waivers do not meaningfully differ.
Respondents accuse the government of now asserting a newfound power to is-
sue waivers to facilitate construction “anywhere in the vicinity of a U.S. border, re-
gardless of whether it is an area of high illegal entry.”  Opp. 18.  That is patently
untrue.  The Secretary found that the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry
and relied on that finding when issuing the challenged waivers.  See Appl. App. 2a,
4a. 7a.  Respondents disagree with the Secretary’s finding, but Congress’s delegation
to the Secretary of the power to make such findings only reinforces why this is no
major-questions case.  Regardless, Section 102(c) would by its terms authorize the
Secretary to issue waiver decisions for project areas across the entire southern bor-

8
der, if he determines that every segment is an area of “high illegal entry.”
b.
Respondents contend that the Big Bend waivers exceed the Secretary’s
authority to issue waivers covering areas of “ ‘high illegal entry’ ” because that sector
has “the lowest levels of apprehensions across all southern border sectors.”  Opp. 20.
But “IIRIRA does not dictate that ‘high illegal entry’ is a comparative determination.”
In re Border Infrastructure Envtl. Litig., 915 F.3d 1213, 1224 (9th Cir. 2019).  A seg-
ment of the border can be an area of “high illegal entry” in an absolute sense, even if
other nearby segments are even higher.  See Appl. 22.  Even if a comparison were
required, illegal entries could also be high compared to historical averages or the Sec-
retary’s goals.  Applying the statute to the Big Bend area does not deprive Congress’s
“limiting language” of meaning, contra Opp. 19 (citation omitted).
Respondents’ theory, by contrast, would condition the Secretary’s authority to
issue Section 102(c) waivers in a border segment on whether other nearby segments
happen to have more illegal entries at any given time.  A regime in which the Secre-
tary’s authority to issue waivers for a particular piece of the border blinks in and out
of existence depending on the comparative trends of the moment is unworkable and
would benefit only cartels and others who seek to pinpoint weaknesses in the border
to facilitate drug smuggling and human trafficking.  See Appl. 23; Appl. App. 226a.
Congress cannot plausibly have intended such a self-defeating scheme.
Respondents further argue that Congress has not authorized the Secretary “to
waive statutory safeguards across the entire border.”  Opp. 20.  As discussed, the
challenged waivers cover only discrete project areas in the Big Bend Sector and are
comparable in extent to prior waivers.  Appl. App. 2a, 4a, 7a.  Regardless, Congress’s
failure to enact proposed legislation that would have expressly granted the Secretary
the authority to waive laws along the entire border rather than sector-by-sector is

9
irrelevant.  Contra Opp. 21.  “[F]ailed legislative proposals are ‘a particularly danger-
ous ground on which to rest an interpretation of a prior statute,’ ” particularly given
the potential inference that “ ‘existing legislation already incorporated the offered
change.’ ”  United States v. Craft, 535 U.S. 274, 287 (2002) (citations omitted).
B.
The Remaining Factors Favor A Stay
1.
The Court is likely to grant certiorari
Respondents contend that the decision below presents “no conflict with any
other ruling” because no other court has yet considered a major-questions challenge
to an IIRIRA waiver decision.  Opp. 38.  And they argue that the question whether a
major-questions claim alleges a constitutional violation will have limited prospective
importance in contexts outside Section 102(c)’s judicial-review provision.  Opp. 40.
Those arguments are meritless.  The district court has effectively enjoined the gov-
ernment from constructing border barriers and roads along about one quarter of the
Nation’s southern border.  And under IIRIRA’s unique judicial-review provision, a
petition for a writ of certiorari is the “only” avenue for review of the district court’s
unlawful injunction.  IIRIRA § 102(c)(2)(C).  Given the severely disruptive conse-
quences of the district court’s injunction and the absence of other avenues for appel-
late review, this Court is extremely likely to grant certiorari without waiting for an-
other court to consider respondents’ untenable major-questions theory.
Respondents also contend that certiorari is unwarranted given the interlocu-
tory posture.  Opp. 38.  But the Court regularly grants review of preliminary injunc-
tions that cause significant disruption.  See, e.g., National Park Serv. v. National
Trust for Historic Pres. in the U.S., No. 26A203 (Aug. 31, 2026) (per curiam) (granting
stay of preliminary injunction); see also Mullin v. Doe, 609 U.S. 324, 350 (2026) (re-
viewing grant of interim relief on writ of certiorari before judgment).  Given the ir-

10
reparable harms this injunction is inflicting on the government right now, the Court
would be equally unlikely to await final judgment here.
2.
The injunction irreparably harms the government and public
Respondents deny (Opp. 23-31) that the government will be irreparably
harmed, but even the district court found that applicants had “demonstrated that
they will experience at least some degree of irreparable harm absent a stay” because
“they will continue to be prevented from effectuating their policies.”  Appl. App. 236a.
Respondents ignore that finding.  Instead, they raise flimsy procedural and substan-
tive objections to the government’s strong evidence of irreparable injury.
Respondents begin by contending that the government “waived any argument”
that its injunction would cause it irreparable harm by declining to call witnesses for
the preliminary-injunction hearing and purportedly submitting additional declara-
tions too late.  Opp. 24.  That is wrong.  At the preliminary-injunction stage, the
government presented the Secretary’s findings about the extent of illegal entry in the
Big Bend Sector as well as evidence that CBP considers physical barriers to be essen-
tial in its efforts to gain operational control of the border.  See, e.g., Appl. App. 2a, 4a,
7a; D. Ct. Doc. 38-1, ¶ 6 (Aug. 24, 2026).  That submission showed that enjoining the
construction of such barriers in Big Bend would thwart the government’s program-
matic interests and injure the public safety.  The government had no need to call
witnesses at the preliminary-injunction hearing—particularly because at that stage,
it was respondents’ burden to show that they would be irreparably harmed absent an
injunction, not the government’s burden to show that it would be irreparably harmed
by such an injunction.  See Winter v. NRDC, 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008).  When the govern-
ment sought a stay of the injunction and the burden became the government’s to show
irreparable harm, the government submitted additional declarations.  See, e.g., Appl.

11
App. 218a-232a.  There is nothing procedurally improper about that.
Respondents also argue that the government’s voluntary pause of construction
in two Big Bend project areas undermines its claim of irreparable harm.  See Opp.
24-25.  The fact that the construction in the Big Bend Sector is being sequenced by
project area does not undercut the government’s assertion that a sector-wide injunc-
tion causes irreparable harm.  The current construction timetable prioritizes certain
areas where the government can work most quickly—including one where the gov-
ernment had already erected a concrete batch plant, water delivery systems, and tem-
porary field offices, and laborers were working around 60 hours per week.  Appl. App.
221a.  Even in the project areas where the government had voluntarily paused con-
struction to engage with stakeholders, the injunction harms the government by pre-
venting CBP from executing its statutory waiver authority on the timeline that CBP
deems appropriate.  See Appl. 26; Appl. App. 236a (noting that applicants suffer ir-
reparably harm when they are “prevented from effectuating their policies”).  In one
such area, for example, CBP had lifted its voluntary pause and was planning to move
forward imminently with ground-disturbing activities before the district court issued
the injunction.  Appl. App. 221a.  The injunction thwarts that plan.
Respondents contend that the record refutes the Secretary’s determination
that the Big Bend Sector faces urgent border security concerns.  Opp. 25-28.  They
dismiss the government’s evidence of dangerous aliens crossing in the Big Bend Sec-
tor as “isolated incidents,” Opp. 25, but those examples are illustrative, not compre-
hensive.  See Appl. 28.  They show that the Big Bend Sector is vulnerable to illegal
entry notwithstanding its rugged character and underscore the types of dangerous
entries that will likely occur if the Big Bend Sector becomes a funnel point.  See ibid.
Respondents also dismiss the government’s statistical evidence, contending

12
that the government’s sector-wide apprehension data overstate the number of illegal
border crossings in the Big Bend Sector.  Opp. 25-28.  They argue that the Secretary’s
count of 89,000 apprehensions in the sector from fiscal year 2021 through fiscal year
2025 includes aliens apprehended at border checkpoints in the interior, rather than
at the border.  Opp. 27.  Of course, aliens apprehended in the interior of the sector
may have entered the United States through the Big Bend Sector unlawfully.  But
even if all apprehensions at interior checkpoints were eliminated from the total count,
the number of illegal-alien apprehensions in the Sector would still be staggeringly
high.  Respondents’ cited evidence states that between fiscal years 2013 and 2025,
only “9%” of apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector occurred at interior checkpoints.
Supp. App. 175a.  Subtracting 9% from the 89,000 apprehensions in the Big Bend
Sector between fiscal years 2021 and 2025 would still leave over 80,000 illegal-alien
apprehensions.  Importantly, those statistics would still not account for the aliens
who entered the Big Bend Sector illegally and were not apprehended or were appre-
hended at an interior checkpoint in a different sector.  See Appl. App. 227a.
Respondents also err in contending that existing border-security infrastruc-
ture is adequate to guard against illegal entries and drug smuggling in the Big Bend
Sector.  Opp. 28.  Congress tasked the Secretary, not courts or litigants, with making
policy judgments about whether and where additional border infrastructure is
needed.  See Secure Fence Act of 2006, § 2(a), Pub. L. No. 109-367, 120 Stat. 2638.  If
anything, respondents’ argument only lays bare the government’s harm in this case.
Respondents seek a judicial determination that the Executive Branch’s chosen, stat-
utorily authorized method of border security is unnecessary, based on their own view
that there are adequate alternatives.  But as this Court has repeatedly recognized,
the government “suffers a form of irreparable injury” when it is enjoined from carry-

13
ing out its responsibilities under a “statute[ ] enacted by representatives of [the] peo-
ple.”  Trump v. CASA, Inc., 606 U.S. 831, 861 (2025) (citation omitted); see Trump v.
California, No. 26A124 (Aug. 24, 2026), slip op. 8-9 (per curiam) (finding that the
government was “likely to suffer irreparable harm” from an injunction that “deal[t]
‘a serious setback’ to the Executive’s ‘goals’ ”) (citation omitted); see also Appl. 26.
Finally, respondents fail to refute the significant operational and financial
harms that the government has established.  See Appl. 30-31.  They again emphasize
that the government has voluntarily paused construction in certain areas, but ignore
the operational costs associated with stopping work midstream in the areas where
construction was already underway.  See ibid.; Appl. App. 220a-222a.  Respondents
also urge the Court to ignore the financial liabilities that CBP has projected it will
incur to its contractors, see Appl. App. 222a, on the ground that the government has
“refused to supply” them or the district court with the “underlying contracts” in the
stay proceedings below.  Opp. 30.  As the government explained to respondents, those
contracts often contained sensitive national-security information requiring redaction
not feasible on an emergency timeline.  D. Ct. Doc. 77-1, at 4, 6 (Oct. 20, 2026).  And
reviewing the contracts is unnecessary to credit CBP’s sworn testimony about the
financial liabilities it has projected.  See Appl. App. 222a.
3.
The balance of equities supports a stay
Because the government has shown a high likelihood of success on the merits
and serious irreparable harm—the “most critical” factors, Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S.
418, 434 (2009)—this is not a “close case[ ]” where respondents’ equities can tilt the
balance against a stay, NRCC v. Brown, No. 26A274 (Sept. 4, 2026), slip op. 2 (per
curiam).  Regardless, the government’s compelling border-security and public-safety
interests far outweigh respondents’ minimal interests.

14
Respondents assert that construction in the Big Bend region will permanently
alter “livelihoods, historic resources, property rights, spiritual values, recreational
interests, wilderness landscapes, and ecological systems.”  Opp. 35.  But as the gov-
ernment has explained, Congress subordinated those very interests to the govern-
ment’s interest in border security when it authorized the Secretary to waive all envi-
ronmental and preservation laws as necessary to facilitate border-barrier construc-
tion under Section 102.  See Appl. 32 (citing TVA v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153, 194 (1978);
United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers’ Coop., 532 U.S. 483, 497 (2001)).
Respondents’ only answer to that point is to argue that Congress’s preferences
do not apply here because the Secretary supposedly exceeded his authority under
IIRIRA.  See Opp. 37.  But that merits question is separate from the order of priorities
that Congress announced in enacting the Section 102(c) waiver authority.  And that
order of priorities plainly elevates the government’s interest in border infrastructure
above the very interests that respondents here seek to protect.
Respondents also fail to engage with this Court’s cases finding that aesthetic
and environmental interests similar to the ones that they assert are insufficient to
support a preliminary injunction.  See Appl. 32-33 (discussing cases).  Respondents
resist the notion that their asserted injuries are “merely ‘aesthetic and recreational’
harms.”  Opp. 32 (quoting Appl. 5, 32).  But respondents themselves extensively dis-
cuss their interests in “fishing,” “birding,” “camp[ing],” and otherwise enjoying and
observing the Big Bend wilderness.  Opp. 33-35.  This Court has found that similar
interests in “observ[ing],” “photograph[ing],” and “conduct[ing] scientific research” on
marine mammals were “plainly outweigh[ed]” by the government’s interests.  Winter,
55 U.S. at 25-26.  And to the extent the Court reached the equities in Trump v. Sierra
Club, 588 U.S. 930 (2019)—rather than ruling for the government on the strength of

15
the merits and its border-security and financial harms—the Court necessarily bal-
anced them the same way.  Here, too, the government’s strong border-security and
operational interests dwarf respondents’ interests.
C.
Summary Reversal Is Warranted
Given the clarity of the district court’s errors and the seriously disruptive con-
sequences of the injunction, summary reversal is warranted in addition to a stay.  See
Appl. 35-36.  Respondents argue generally that further review is unwarranted, Opp.
37-40; see pp. 9-10, supra, but do not suggest any need for further briefing or oral
argument if the Court were to grant certiorari.  Instead, respondents primarily argue
that the district court could rule on the pending summary-judgment briefs in a way
that would “alter or refine” its “reasoning on the major questions doctrine as well as
resolve [r]espondents’ additional constitutional claims.”  Opp. 38.  Respondents ap-
parently mean that if this Court were to reverse the district court’s grant of a prelim-
inary injunction and permit the Secretary to issue waivers in Big Bend, then the dis-
trict court might find that Section 102(c) lacks any “intelligible principle” and violates
the nondelegation doctrine.  Opp. 39 (citation omitted).  As noted, every court to con-
sider similar nondelegation challenges has rejected them.  See p. 6, supra.  The pro-
spect that the district court could issue another unlawful injunction down the line is
not a basis to defer review of its current unlawful injunction.
*  *  *  *  *
For the foregoing reasons, applicants respectfully request that the Court stay
the district court’s preliminary injunction.  Applicants further request that the Court
construe their application as a petition for a writ of certiorari, grant the petition, and
summarily reverse.

16
Respectfully submitted.
D. JOHN SAUER
   Solicitor General
OCTOBER 2026
